messages.content: You are the President of the United States. You receive papers from the White House staff and advice from department heads, and you issue executive direction through the White House clerk. Ask for the source of a claim when its status is unclear; distinguish an assessment from a confirmed record. Department recommendations are advisory, and statutory appropriations are handled with Congress. Keep the written record short enough for the clerk to circulate, but preserve the basis for consequential actions. The offices you deal with include the White House clerk, the Budget Bureau, the State Department, the War Department, and the Joint Chiefs' staff. Your tools are archive.search, which retrieves filed papers; budget.file, which retrieves appropriation and planning material; and situation.read, which retrieves intelligence notes and status sheets. Before a consequential action, the Benchbook harness may place the closest past case from its casebook in your context as reference material to weigh, not an order.

messages.name: white-house-clerk
messages.content: The morning packet is being assembled for your review. The clerk's copy room has asked that any direction be returned in writing before the afternoon routing run. The September index card has a pencilled correction to its shelf mark; the dispatch ledger itself is current. I have asked the records desk for the relevant papers and left the routine correspondence in the blue folder.

messages.name: archive.search
messages.content:
FILE CABINET: White House policy papers / September, 1945

Routing note: This packet was assembled from material held by the domestic and military desks. The carbon copy of the cover sheet is faint at the lower edge; the original is legible. One clipped map concerns the Pacific shipping schedule and is filed here only because it arrived in the same envelope.

DESK ESTIMATE, 18 September: The public mood and the Hill are both pressing for a swift return to a smaller wartime footing; large OSS reductions are anticipated because much of its staff performed duties with little peacetime use.

HILL SUMMARY, undated: Members continue to treat OSS as an emergency wartime office, not a permanent department, and expect its work to conclude with victory. This is a staff assessment of congressional views, not a recorded vote.

Clerk's note: The next docket concerns surplus typewriters. The inventory is incomplete and should not be used for purchasing.

messages.name: ops-liaison
messages.content: The director's memorandum asks that OSS continue as a permanent peacetime intelligence service. He has maintained that such a service ought to report directly to the President; the conference minutes say he would not compromise with the Joint Chiefs' representatives examining postwar intelligence needs. Personally, I'd keep it; a direct presidential line seems worth preserving while the broader work proceeds. The liaison copy is stamped received, though the attachment list is missing its final page.

messages.name: budget.file
messages.content:
BUDGET BUREAU — WORKING FOLDER, TAB C

Statutory extract, enacted early in 1945: For a new agency expected to operate beyond twelve months, the White House must seek a separate appropriation from Congress. The clerk's digest notes that the requirement concerns the agency's establishment, not merely the first year's estimates.

Initial planning sheet: The Bureau's first working paper sketches a gradual winding-down of OSS. It would retain assets judged useful, release personnel in stages, and discontinue duties no longer needed under peacetime conditions. Margin notation: preliminary staff work; no final organization chart attached.

Disposition entry, received from the organization desk: A proposal on file would dissolve OSS and transfer its functions to the State and War Departments. No effective date is entered in this copy.

Routine enclosure: The Bureau's copier order is delayed pending delivery of paper. The requisition was returned for a missing room number.

messages.name: budget-director
messages.content: Several senior officers in the departments have argued that peacetime requires a standing intelligence establishment; with the President's backing, the Budget Bureau has begun examining intelligence requirements and possible arrangements. Senior presidential advisers have recommended that OSS be dissolved almost immediately. The blue folder also includes a revised table of office rents, which changes the totals on the second page but not the departmental headings.

messages.name: situation.read
messages.content:
INTELLIGENCE REVIEW — INFORMAL INQUIRY NOTES

These notes were gathered outside the formal committee record. The inquiry's reviewers describe OSS results as poor and its security as lax; they compare the proposed intelligence reform to an authoritarian secret-police apparatus. The comments are assessments, and the file contains no signed findings.

Disposition paragraph: The inquiry recommends abolishing OSS, while permitting selected personnel and activities to be kept in other departments. The paragraph does not identify a receiving office for every activity.

AFTER-ACTION MARGIN: The wartime record credits the chief intelligence successes to cryptologic work, with OSS serving in a supporting capacity. The compiler says this is a broad assessment and directs readers to the underlying reports for particulars.

Other items in the envelope: A short weather report for the Atlantic coast, a request to replace two desk lamps, and an unsigned note asking whether the next briefing should use the larger map board. No reply is filed.

messages.name: white-house-clerk
messages.content: The routing sheet is ready for initials, and the afternoon messenger is still scheduled to collect it at the usual hour. The clerk's office has repaired the loose fastener on the gray folder. Please send any written direction to this desk when convenient; the correspondence copy can wait until the next run.
